Abstract (Crossref, read this round): 'We use information from over 2 million trading strategies randomly generated using real data ... compute t-statistic thresholds that control for multiple hypothesis testing ... at 3.8 and 3.4 for time-series and cross-sectional regressions, respectively. We estimate the expected proportion of false rejections that researchers would produce if they failed to account for multiple hypothesis testing to be about 45%.' The span: 'generate over 2 million trading strategies from real data, infer the properties of the strategies researchers could have studied, compute multiple-testing t-statistic thresholds of 3.8 for time-series and 3.4 for cross-sectional regressions, and estimate that researchers who ignored multiple testing would produce about 45% false rejections' — matches (the 'generate ... from real data' is the paper's 'randomly generated using real data'). Grade B; the contest is JKP (span 2). PASS.

The row now reads 'For an AR(1) series with \(\phi \gt 0\), the iid bootstrap understates the standard error of the mean by \(\sqrt{(1+\phi)/(1-\phi)}\)', grade T, 'Derived in section 3'. Re-derived: for x_t = phi x_{t-1} + e_t, |phi| < 1, gamma(h) = sigma^2 phi^|h|/(1 - phi^2), so sum_h gamma(h) = sigma^2/(1-phi)^2 and the ratio of the long-run to the iid variance gamma(0) is (1+phi)/(1-phi) (section 3 displays exactly this chain). The iid bootstrap variance of the mean is gamma-hat(0)/T, so true SE / iid SE = sqrt((1+phi)/(1-phi)): 1.732 at phi = 0.5 (ratio 3), 1.5275 at 0.4, exactly 1 at phi = 0 (no understatement, hence the strict inequality is right), and 0.577 at phi = -0.5 (ratio 1/3), where the iid value is 1.73 times too large. For phi > 0 the ratio exceeds 1 because 1 + phi > 1 - phi, so 'understates' holds for every phi in (0, 1): the row is now exactly true in its stated domain. The quoted factor is the large-T limit that section 3 displays (T Var(x-bar) -> ...); at T = 500 and phi = 0.5 the exact finite-sample factor is sqrt(2.992) = 1.730 against 1.732 (2.992 = 3 - 1/125, the T Var(d-bar) printed by Problem E4), so the table is right as an asymptotic statement and consistent with the page's own T = 500 numbers. (1) Given the data, the reference law of T^(-1/2) sum_t eps_t d_t has variance T^(-1) sum_t d_t^2 (eps_t = +-1 i.i.d., mean 0, variance 1), so (H1) gives gamma(0). (2) The reference law is symmetric about 0, so its 95% quantile of |.| equals its 97.5% quantile of the signed sum; under (H2) both tend to the 0.975 quantile of N(0, gamma(0)). (3) Quantile identity checked numerically (remark35_limits.out section 1, g = 2.5): 95% quantile of |N(0,g)| = sqrt(g) z_0.975 = 3.0989751615, 97.5% quantile of N(0,g) = 3.0989751615 (equal); z_0.975 = 1.9599639845 (so 1.96 is the 97.5% quantile of N(0,1)). The literal misreading (97.5% quantile of |N(0,1)| = 2.2414027276) is not what the sentence now says. (4) (H3) gives T^(-1/2) sum d_t -> N(0, sigma2_LR); sigma2_LR/gamma(0) = (1+phi)/(1-phi) = 3 at phi = 0.5 and 1.857142857 at phi = 0.3 (remark35_limits.out section 2: direct sums over |h| <= 4000 agree with the closed form). (5) The limit: 2(1 - Phi(1.96 sqrt(gamma0/sigma2))) = 0.2577998945 at phi = 0.5 (page form 2(1 - Phi(1.132)) = 0.2576344344, rounds to 0.258) and 0.1503640418 at phi = 0.3 (page form 2(1 - Phi(1.438)) = 0.1504340541, rounds to 0.150) (remark35_limits.out section 3). rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L03.html Lemma 2.3 (line 102) and its proof; card S7-c217
rows.evidence: unchanged since 1b3ef73 (git diff checked); round-18 evidence: Re-derived. (a) p_(k) <= kq/m iff at least k p-values are <= kq/m: if p_(k) <= kq/m then p_(1..k) are all <= kq/m, so N(k) >= k; if N(k) >= k then the k-th smallest is <= kq/m. Hence R = max{k : N(k) >= k}. (b) If R >= 1, a rejected H_i has p_i <= p_(R) <= Rq/m. Conversely, if p_i <= Rq/m but p_i = p_(j) with j > R, then p_(j) <= Rq/m <= jq/m, so N(j) >= j, contradicting the maximality of R; the zero case is handled (N(1) >= 1 forces R >= 1). (c) Raising a p-value can only lower each N(k), so the largest k with N(k) >= k cannot increase. Numerical spot check (scratch py/spotchecks_r12.py): for 2,000 random p-vectors (m = 10, q = 0.05, mixed scales) the BH rejection set equals {i : p_i <= R q/m} with R = max{k : N(k) >= k} (0 violations), and R does not increase when one randomly chosen p-value is raised (0 violations). Ties: the proof uses the k-th smallest p-value, so ties do not change the count.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L03.html Proposition 5.3 (line 281) and its proof; card S7-c218
rows.evidence: unchanged since 1b3ef73 (git diff checked); round-18 evidence: Re-derived for rho in [0,1). Given z_i = t, the joint Gaussian (W, z_i) gives W | z_i = t ~ N(sqrt(rho)(t - mu_i), 1 - rho), stochastically increasing in t for rho >= 0 (the constant case rho = 0 is trivially monotone). The other coordinates are z_j = sqrt(rho) W + sqrt(1-rho) eps_j + mu_j with eps_j independent of (W, z_i), so P(z in D' | z_i = t) = E[g(W) | z_i = t], g non-increasing for a decreasing D' (translating all z_j by a common amount). Hence t -> P(z in D' | z_i = t) is non-increasing, which is PRDS (Definition 5.1) on every subset. Numerical spot check (scratch py/spotchecks_r12.py, Monte Carlo 600,000 draws, rho = 0.5, m = 3, D = {p_2 >= 1/2, p_3 >= 1/2}, an increasing set in p-space): P(D | z_1 near t) falls from 0.556 at t = -1 to 0.033 at t = 2 (non-increasing in t), and P(D | p_1 near u) rises from 0.054 at u = 0.05 to 0.708 at u = 0.95 (non-decreasing in u): the PRDS inequality holds in the numerical check. (An earlier attempt used the z-increasing set {z_2 > 0, z_3 > 0}; that set is not an increasing set of p-values, so it was discarded.)

rows.evidence: Span text (new): 'Roquain and Verzelen show that an estimated null cannot always stand in for the true one: when the nulls are Gaussian with unknown mean and variance, a procedure that asymptotically matches Benjamini-Hochberg run with the true null exists if and only if the number of false nulls is of order less than N/log N, where N is the number of tests.' Crossref 10.1214/21-aos2141 (Annals of Statistics 50(2) 1095-1123, issued 2022-04-01; read this round): 'We explore this issue in the setting where the null distributions are Gaussian with unknown rescaling parameters (mean and variance) whereas the alternative distributions are let arbitrary. In that case, an oracle procedure is the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure applied with the true (unknown) null distribution and we aim at building a procedure that asymptotically mimics the performances of the oracle (AMO in short). Our main result establishes a phase transition at the sparsity boundary n/log(n): an AMO procedure exists if and only if the number of false nulls is of order less than n/log(n), where n is the total number of tests.' Attribution, model, quantifier and boundary all match. 'Cannot always stand in' is the impossibility half of the result. The span's own clause pins the notion to asymptotic oracle-matching. rows.location: L03.html line 409 (Efron span: efron2004large, Abstract, grade B); card S7-c128 front and back (the Efron claim); line 599 clause
rows.evidence: Efron (2004) Abstract, read this round (OpenAlex, DOI 10.1198/016214504000000089): 'Current scientific techniques in genomics and image processing routinely produce hypothesis testing problems with hundreds or thousands of cases to consider simultaneously ... it allows empirical estimation of an appropriate null hypothesis. The empirical null may be considerably more dispersed than the usual theoretical null distribution that would be used for any one case considered separately.' The span's two clauses match. Counter-evidence search: Jin and Cai (2007), JASA 102(478) 495-506, DOI 10.1198/016214507000000167 (not in registry; OpenAlex abstract read: estimators 'uniformly consistent over a wide class of parameters'). Its non-sparse critique, as quoted by Kotekal and Gao (2025, pp. 4-5, citing pp. 495-496 of Jin and Cai): 'In such settings, Efron's (2004) approach does not perform well, and it is not hard to show that the estimators of the null are generally inconsistent' (the original page was not readable here; the quotation is K&G's). Kotekal and Gao (2025) bear on that critique: consistent estimation of the null location holds for k < n/2 - omega(sqrt n), which includes non-sparse k = cn with c < 1/2. Cai and Jin (2010), AoS 38(1) 100-145 (DOI 10.1214/09-aos696; Crossref abstract read): minimax rates for estimating the null density and the nonnull proportion. Efron (2007), DOI 10.1198/016214506000001211 (OpenAlex abstract read): a caveat on the null distribution under correlation, not a contest of the 2004 claims. Verdict: the span's claim is attributed to Efron, is supported by the 2007 and 2010 work and, in the regime the page's words 'many simultaneous tests' most naturally cover, by K&G (2025). The non-sparse critique is a named scope limit that the page omits. PASS with a non-blocking flag: state Efron's sparsity assumption ('most tests null') or cite Jin and Cai (2007) and Kotekal and Gao (2025) as two-sided counter-evidence (registry flags RF32, RF31).

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L03.html line 599 (bullet 4), line 409 (Roquain span); card S7-c128; Kotekal and Gao 2025 (not in registry)
rows.evidence: Question: do Kotekal and Gao (arXiv 2401.06350v2; IEEE TIT 71(3) 2075-2103; DOI 10.1109/tit.2025.3529457) contest a claim of the page? Read: abstract (arXiv listing) and full text (PDF v2, 48 pp.; the introduction discusses Efron, Jin and Cai (2007) and the regime k ~ n; no citation of Roquain and Verzelen (2022)). Their result: consistent estimation of the null location is possible iff n/2 - k = omega(sqrt n); of the scale, for every k < n/2. Their target is consistent estimation of (theta, sigma), not oracle matching of the BH procedure; they do not state an AMO result, an FDR result or any limit on FDR procedures. So K&G do not contest the AMO boundary of Roquain and Verzelen, which the page now states (span: 'a procedure that asymptotically matches Benjamini-Hochberg run with the true null exists if and only if ...'; card: 'match the oracle ... (Benjamini-Hochberg run with the true null)'). Roquain and Verzelen themselves separate the two aims: 'In light of our impossibility results, we also pursue the less stringent aim of building a nonparametric confidence region for the null distribution' (Crossref abstract). The page's lead clause 'an estimated null cannot always stand in for the true one' is qualified by that span, so it does not state an estimation limit. The round-18 target ('the limit on estimating it') is no longer on the page. PASS. Freshness flag (non-blocking): K&G 2025 is the estimation counterpart and should be cited when the page discusses estimating the null (registry flag RF31).

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L03.html line 95 (figcaption of the bh-geometry figure)
rows.evidence: The caption says: 'BH finds the last rank whose p-value lies on or under the rising line and rejects everything up to it, including smaller p-values that sit above their own line.' The second half is a claim about every state, and it is false in most of them. Over the 39 grid values of q (0.010 to 0.200), a rank k <= k* with p(k) > kq/m exists only at q = 0.050 (k* = 5, rank 4). At the other 38 values (for example q = 0.010, k* = 1 with no carried rank; readout 'BH rejects 1 of 10'), nothing above its line is rejected. The caption therefore fails 'true in every state' (BUILDER_RULES 6.4), while the readout itself is correct in every state. Verified by the sweep (R19-cmd-drive-compare-figs) and by the carried-rank count (script): 38 of 39 states have no carried rank.
